407.title: Not by bread alone (Deuteronomy 8:1–3)
407.hook: the hunger in the wilderness taught them to live by every word
407.carry: carried, even when it didn't feel like it
407.howItsDone: Some Christians fast at certain times, such as Lent, Fridays or before communion, and Orthodox and Catholic Christians keep set fasting days; this verse is a common way to explain why.

segments.voice: Yesterday: ebed, and some of the hardest laws in the Bible, read without defending or skipping. Your line: read the hard parts honestly.

Four in the afternoon, and lunch never happened. First a low hum in the stomach, then a tightness, then a short answer to someone who didn't deserve it. Hunger is honest. Now stretch that to forty years of depending, morning after morning, on food that came with the dew and spoiled if it was saved. Moses, near the end of his life, looks back at those years in Deuteronomy, and says something surprising about the hunger. It wasn't an accident. It was a lesson.
screen: `FOUR O'CLOCK, NO LUNCH.` → `HUNGER IS HONEST.` → `THE HUNGER WAS A LESSON.`

segments.voice: Moses says, in the King James Bible: "thou shalt remember all the way which the LORD thy God led thee these forty years in the wilderness." And then: "he humbled thee, and suffered thee to hunger, and fed thee with manna, which thou knewest not, neither did thy fathers know; that he might make thee know that man doth not live by bread only, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of the LORD doth man live." Look at the order. First the hunger. Then the manna, a food nobody had ever seen, so nobody could take credit for it. Then the lesson: you need bread, yes, and you also need something bread can't give, the word that comes from God. Moses adds a tender detail in the next verse: in all those forty years, your clothes didn't wear out, and your feet didn't swell. Carried, even when it didn't feel like it. Later, in the Gospels, Jesus is alone in the wilderness for forty days, fasting, and he's hungry. The tempter says: if you're the Son of God, turn these stones into bread. Jesus answers with this verse from Deuteronomy, in slightly different words. In the King James Bible's Matthew: "Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of God." Christians who keep fasts, in Lent or before communion or at other times, often reach for this verse to explain them: not to punish the body, but to let a little hunger remind them what else they live on.

segments.voice: Notice what you're hungry for beyond food: rest, attention, being known, a word from God. Some people let a small hunger, one skipped snack or dessert, be the reminder; only if it's safe for you, and if you're pregnant, unwell, or have any history with food that makes this hard, skip the hunger and keep just the listening. If you pray, turn each pang into a short prayer.
Manna. The food nobody had seen before, given each morning in the wilderness, to teach that man does not live by bread alone.

408.title: Choose life (Deuteronomy 30:15–20)
408.hook: I set before you life and death: choose life
408.carry: near, in your mouth and in your heart
408.howItsDone: Some Christians turn to Deuteronomy 30 when speaking about daily decisions and moral choices, and Paul quotes 'the word is nigh thee' from this chapter in Romans 10.

segments.voice: Yesterday: manna, and a hunger that taught a lesson: not by bread alone. Your line: carried, even when it didn't feel like it.
screen: `CARRIED, EVEN WHEN IT DIDN'T FEEL LIKE IT.`

segments.voice: Plenty of the choices that shape a life don't feel like choices at all. They feel like Tuesday. Text back, or let it slide. Bed, or one more episode. The true thing, or the easy one. Each one is tiny, but laid end to end, they become a direction. Moses is near the end of his great speech in Deuteronomy. Now he boils it all down to a single choice, and sets it in front of his people like two plates on a table.
screen: `CHOICES THAT FEEL LIKE TUESDAY.` → `END TO END, A DIRECTION.` → `TWO PLATES ON A TABLE.`

segments.voice: Here's how Moses says it, in the King James Bible: "See, I have set before thee this day life and good, and death and evil." A few verses on, he calls witnesses: "I call heaven and earth to record this day against you, that I have set before you life and death, blessing and cursing: therefore choose life, that both thou and thy seed may live." In Hebrew: u-vacharta ba-chayyim, and you shall choose life. Chayyim, life, is plural in form, and some readers hear in that plural that life is always more than one thing: breath and family and land and God, all at once. It's the same word as in the Jewish toast, l'chaim, to life. Notice what Moses doesn't do. He doesn't choose for them. He sets it out, and he pleads. And just before this, he says how possible it is. It isn't too hard for you, or far away, up in heaven or across the sea. "But the word is very nigh unto thee, in thy mouth, and in thy heart, that thou mayest do it." Then Moses says what life is: loving God, listening to his voice, holding on to him, "for he is thy life, and the length of thy days." Paul quotes the word is nigh thee in his letter to the Romans, and some Christian readers hear an echo of the two ways in Jesus' words about two roads, one narrow. And notice how often Moses says this day. The choice isn't saved for the end. It's on the table today.

segments.voice: Think ahead through the rest of your day and find one small fork, two plates on the table, where one choice leaves you or someone else a little more alive: a walk instead of the scroll, the kind answer instead of the clever one. 409.title: Moses sees the land (Deuteronomy 34)
409.hook: on Mount Nebo he sees the land he'll never enter, and dies
409.howItsDone: Christian pilgrims visit Mount Nebo in Jordan, where a memorial church stands, and some preachers turn to Deuteronomy 34 at funerals and farewells to speak of work handed on to others.

segments.voice: Yesterday: choose life, two plates set before a people, and the word close at hand. Your line: near, in your mouth and in your heart.
screen: `NEAR, IN YOUR MOUTH AND IN YOUR HEART.`

segments.voice: An old man climbs a mountain. He's a hundred and twenty. Forty of those years he's spent walking a whole people through the desert: complaints and manna, golden calves and giants, the long funeral march of a generation. Now they're camped by the Jordan River, one crossing away from the land. But he won't cross. He's been told. So he climbs Mount Nebo, east of the river, and at the top God shows him everything: the hills to the north, the valleys, the palm-tree city of Jericho, all the way to the sea in the west.
screen: `A HUNDRED AND TWENTY YEARS OLD.` → `ONE RIVER AWAY.` → `UP NEBO, TO SEE.`

segments.voice: Then God says, in the King James Bible: "I have caused thee to see it with thine eyes, but thou shalt not go over thither." Why can't he go? Back in Numbers, at a place called Meribah, Moses struck the rock twice with his rod instead of speaking to it as God told him, and he was told then that he wouldn't lead the people in. Readers still argue about whether that seems fair. The text doesn't argue. "So Moses the servant of the LORD died there in the land of Moab." Then a mysterious detail: he buried him, the text says, in a valley, and tradition reads he as God, "but no man knoweth of his sepulchre unto this day." No grave to visit, no shrine. The people go on without a monument. The chapter adds that "his eye was not dim, nor his natural force abated." He didn't wear out. He was simply finished. It ends with an epitaph: there arose not a prophet since in Israel like Moses, whom the LORD knew face to face. Who wrote a chapter describing Moses' own death? Jewish tradition, in the Talmud, offers more than one answer: some sages said Joshua wrote the last verses; others said Moses wrote them himself, in tears. Today Mount Nebo is in Jordan, and pilgrims climb it to look out over the same view. Moses gave his whole life to a promise he saw but didn't enter. Christians remember that he does appear, much later, on another mountain, talking with Jesus at the transfiguration.

segments.voice: Think of something you're working toward that will likely outlast you: children, students, a garden, a cause, a tree you planted. Picture it years from now, flourishing, without you in the picture, and like Moses on the mountain, let it be enough to have seen it begin. If you pray, bless it, and the people who'll carry it on.

410.title: Why Christians read the Torah
410.hook: Jesus quoted Deuteronomy in the desert and summed the law in two commandments from it
410.howItsDone: Most churches read from the Old Testament, including the Torah, in worship, and many Christians learn Jesus' summary of the law, the two great commandments, by heart.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Mount Nebo, and Moses seeing the land he would never enter. Your line: seeing is enough.

Plagues and Passover. Manna and mountains. For five weeks now, this path has walked through Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers and Deuteronomy. A fair question, on a Christian path: why? Most churches don't keep the food laws, and none offer animal sacrifices. Here's one place to start. When Jesus was alone in the desert, hungry and tempted three times, he answered three times. And every answer was a quotation from one book. Deuteronomy.
screen: `FIVE WEEKS IN THE BOOKS OF MOSES.` → `A FAIR QUESTION: WHY?` → `THREE ANSWERS FROM ONE BOOK.`

segments.voice: Torah is usually translated law, but it's closer to teaching, or instruction: the way a parent points a child down the right road. It's the Jewish name for the first five books of the Bible, the books of Moses. For Jesus, these were scripture; he grew up hearing them read in the synagogue. In the desert he answered the tempter with them: man shall not live by bread alone; thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God; worship God and serve him only. Near the end of his life, someone asks him which commandment is the greatest, and he reaches into the Torah twice. In Matthew's Gospel, in the King James Bible: "Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind. This is the first and great commandment. And the second is like unto it, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself. On these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets." The first comes from the Shema in Deuteronomy, the line right after hear, O Israel. The second is from Leviticus. Hang: like a door on its two hinges, everything else swings on these two. Jesus also said, "Think not that I am come to destroy the law, or the prophets: I am not come to destroy, but to fulfil." Christians have understood that in different ways. Catholic, Orthodox and many Protestant teachers distinguish the moral law, which still guides, from ceremonial laws they see as fulfilled in Christ. Lutherans often speak of law and gospel, the law showing our need and the gospel meeting it. But nearly all of them read these books as their own scripture, shared with the Jewish people, who read them first.
screen: `TORAH: TEACHING, NOT JUST LAW.` · `THREE ANSWERS FROM DEUTERONOMY.` · `TWO HINGES: GOD, AND NEIGHBOR.` · `NOT TO DESTROY, BUT TO FULFIL.` · then, large: `ON THESE TWO COMMANDMENTS HANG ALL THE LAW.`

segments.voice: Hold the two hinges. On one breath, call the first to mind: love God with all your heart and soul and mind; on the next, the second: love your neighbor as yourself. Notice which one feels closer to your life today, and if you pray, ask for help with the harder one.

411.title: Block close: the wilderness road
411.hook: slaves, sea, manna, mountain, calf, and forty years of being carried
411.howItsDone: Some Christians describe hard seasons as 'wilderness' times, and Lent's forty days recall Jesus' forty days in the wilderness, which some readers link to Israel's forty years.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Torah, teaching, and all the law hung on two commandments. Your line: on these two hang all.

Five weeks ago, this path opened on a people making bricks for a king who had forgotten them. Since then: two midwives who said no. A basket in the reeds. A bush on fire that didn't burn up, and a name, I AM. Plagues, and blood on the doorposts. A sea that opened. Thunder on a mountain, ten words, a golden calf, the back of God passing by. Corners of fields, a jubilee horn, twelve spies, a talking donkey, and an old man on Nebo looking at a land he'd never enter. Today, a look back down that road.
screen: `BRICKS FOR A KING WHO FORGOT.` → `A SEA, A MOUNTAIN, A CALF.` → `TODAY, A LOOK BACK.`

segments.voice: The Hebrew name for the book of Numbers is Bemidbar: in the wilderness. For these four books, that's where the people mostly are. Not in Egypt anymore, not in the land yet. In between. They complain about the water, the food, Moses, the giants. They make a calf the moment Moses is late. A whole generation is too afraid to go in. Read these books looking for heroes, and almost everyone disappoints, including, at Meribah, Moses himself. But read again and notice who keeps showing up. Manna morning after morning, even after they grumbled. Water from a rock. A pillar of cloud by day and fire by night. Clothes that didn't wear out. Here's how Moses sums it up in Deuteronomy, in the King James Bible: "in the wilderness, where thou hast seen how that the LORD thy God bare thee, as a man doth bear his son, in all the way that ye went, until ye came into this place." Bare thee: carried you, like a father carrying a tired child on his shoulders the last mile home. That's the thread through the whole road. Not that the people were strong, or faithful, or patient. They mostly weren't. It's that they were carried. Christians read their own lives in this road too. Paul, writing to the church in Corinth, says these wilderness stories were written down as examples for later readers. Rescued from slavery, but not home yet; fed one day at a time; failing, and carried anyway. Tomorrow the path opens the songbook those carried people and their children would one day sing: the Psalms.

412.title: The tree by the water (Psalm 1)
412.hook: the happy person is like a tree planted by rivers
412.howItsDone: Christians pray the Psalms in the Liturgy of the Hours, in the Anglican Daily Office and in personal devotions; some monastic communities pray the whole Psalter each week.

segments.voice: Yesterday: bemidbar, the wilderness road from slavery to the edge of the land. Your line: carried through the desert.

Monks chant them in the dark before dawn. People whisper them at bedsides. A hundred and fifty poems: praise and complaint, thanks and rage, songs for a crowd and songs for one person awake at night. The Psalms: a songbook, not a story. For fifty days, the path reads them and the wisdom books. And the very first psalm, the front door to the whole collection, opens with a picture: a tree, growing beside a stream.
screen: `A NEW BLOCK: THE PSALMS.` → `A HUNDRED AND FIFTY SONGS.` → `THE FRONT DOOR IS A TREE.`

segments.voice: Psalm one begins, in the King James Bible: "Blessed is the man that walketh not in the counsel of the ungodly, nor standeth in the way of sinners, nor sitteth in the seat of the scornful." Notice the slow drift. Walking, then standing, then sitting. Passing bad advice, lingering, then pulling up a chair as a scoffer yourself. Nobody sits down all at once. Blessed here is the Hebrew ashrei, which also means happy, or how fortunate: the book of praises opens with oh, the happiness of. Then: "But his delight is in the law of the LORD; and in his law doth he meditate day and night." Meditate, in Hebrew hagah, is a sound word, used elsewhere for a dove's moan and a lion's growl over its prey. To meditate on scripture was to murmur it under your breath, over and over, chewing on it. And then the picture: "And he shall be like a tree planted by the rivers of water, that bringeth forth his fruit in his season; his leaf also shall not wither." In a dry land, a tree beside an irrigation channel is a small miracle. Its roots go down to water nobody sees. It still has seasons; it doesn't fruit all year. But it doesn't dry up in the heat. The psalm ends with the other kind of life, which it calls chaff, the husks that blow away on the threshing floor. Two ways, the last verse says: the way of the righteous, and the way of the ungodly, right at the door of the book. Saint Benedict's Rule for monks spreads all hundred and fifty psalms across each week, and some communities still keep that weekly round.

413.title: What is man? (Psalm 8)
413.hook: the moon and stars, and yet God is mindful of us
413.carry: what are we, that you care?
413.howItsDone: Christians pray Psalm 8 in daily prayer and at services that give thanks for creation, and the letter to the Hebrews (chapter 2) reads it as pointing to Jesus.

segments.voice: Yesterday: ashrei, the first psalm, and a tree with its roots in hidden water. Your line: planted by the water.

Go outside on a clear night, away from the streetlights, and look up long enough for your eyes to adjust. First a few stars. Then dozens. Then a haze too many to count, and maybe the pale smear of the Milky Way. Out there it's easy to feel two things at once: very small, and strangely more awake than all week. Long ago, someone stood under that same sky, with no telescopes and no streetlights, and the psalm's heading names him David. He wrote down a question people are still asking.
screen: `A CLEAR NIGHT, NO STREETLIGHTS.` → `VERY SMALL, AND VERY AWAKE.` → `THE SAME SKY, LONG AGO.`

segments.voice: Psalm eight opens and closes with the same line, in the King James Bible: "O LORD our Lord, how excellent is thy name in all the earth!" Praise as bookends. In between, the question: "When I consider thy heavens, the work of thy fingers, the moon and the stars, which thou hast ordained; What is man, that thou art mindful of him? and the son of man, that thou visitest him?" Notice the work of thy fingers. Not God's arm, not his mighty hand. Fingers, like someone doing fine embroidery. The whole night sky is fingerwork. Next to that, what are we? A breath. A speck. And yet God is mindful of us, remembers us, comes to see us. Then the psalm turns the other way: "For thou hast made him a little lower than the angels, and hast crowned him with glory and honour." The Hebrew word there is elohim, which can mean God or heavenly beings. The King James says angels, and so does the letter to the Hebrews when it quotes this verse; some translations say a little lower than God. Small, and crowned. And given dominion, the psalm says, over the sheep and oxen, the birds and the fish. Some readers hear in that a charge to care for the world, not only to rule it. Hebrews hears these verses fulfilled in Jesus, crowned with glory after being made low.

segments.voice: Look up, through a window or outside; if it's daytime, the stars are still there behind the blue. Let yourself feel small, one person on one planet circling one star among more than anyone can count, and then let the second half of the psalm in: and yet, remembered, cared for. If you pray, ask the psalm's question out loud: what am I, that you care?
Enosh. One of the Hebrew words for a human being, the psalmist's word for how small we are under the stars, and yet remembered.
